\chapter{And, Or, But}
\label{ch:hi-flat-joins}
\hlchaptermodality{68}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two Hindi sentences with aur, offer a choice with yaa, and take something back with lekin.}

Complete HI-R68-three-joins and fill the same slot three ways with chay and dudh: added, offered, contradicted.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aur]{\emph{aur} — \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}, and the one letter this book still owes you}

\label{lesson:HI-C68-aur}



\begin{quote}
You can name two drinks: \emph{chāy}, \emph{dūdh}. You can ask for either. What you cannot do — after sixty-seven chapters — is put both in one sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \emph{aur}}
\begin{quote}
\emph{aur} — \textbf{and}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{mujhe chāy aur dūdh pasand hai.} — \textbf{I like tea and milk.}
\end{quote}

\emph{aur} stands BETWEEN the two things and changes neither of them. That is the whole rule, and it is why this one word is worth more than any noun in the book: every word you have learned in sixty-seven chapters just doubled its reach.

It joins two whole sentences the same way, and that is the use that matters most — a written message of thirty words is a message with \emph{aur} in it.

\emph{aur} comes down from Sanskrit \emph{apara}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{other, further}.\textquotedblright{} Hindi's word for \emph{one more} started as a word for \emph{the other one}. Marathi did the identical thing out of a different Sanskrit word, \emph{anya}, and English does it from the third side: \emph{another} is \emph{an other}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word — one is still owed to you}
Look at the headword above and then use the word by ear. Its opening vowel is the independent \emph{au}, and \textbf{this book has not taught that letter}. You have met it exactly once, inside \emph{aurat}, and no writing lesson has ever drawn it.

So this lesson is deliberately \textbf{gloss-first}: the Devanagari sits in the headword where you can start to recognise its shape, the body says the word in Roman letters, and the debt is written down rather than hidden. Learn \emph{aur} now by ear — it is far too useful to wait for — and the letter will come.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy aur dūdh} — tea and milk
  \item \emph{mujhe chāy aur dūdh pasand hai}
  \item which letter of \emph{aur} you have not been taught — \textbf{the opening \emph{au}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{aur} stand, and what does it change? (\textbf{Between the two pieces; nothing}.) What did it mean in Sanskrit? (\textbf{Other, further}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%94\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: aur}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… yā …]{… \hi{या} … (\emph{yā}) — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C68-ya}



\begin{quote}
One lesson ago you got \emph{aur}, which adds. Say \emph{chāy aur dūdh}. Now the word that does the opposite: it puts two things side by side and asks the listener to take exactly one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{या}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{या}} — \emph{yā} — \textbf{or}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{या} \hi{दूध}?} — \emph{chāy yā dūdh?} — \textbf{Tea or milk?}
\end{quote}

It sits exactly where \emph{aur} sat. The two are a matched pair: same slot, opposite job. \emph{aur} hands you both; \textbf{\hi{या}} makes you choose.

Two syllables of good news about the writing: \textbf{\hi{या}} is \textbf{\hi{य}} plus the long \textbf{\hi{ा}}, and you have had both for a long time. Unlike \emph{aur}, you can write this one today.

Offering a choice is a whole conversational move, not just a word. \textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{या} \hi{दूध}?} is a complete, polite offer with no verb in it at all, and it is how a host asks and how an examiner's role-play begins.

\textbf{\hi{या}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{वा}} (\emph{vā}), the ancient particle of alternatives, with the \emph{v-} softened to \emph{y-}. Latin kept the same particle as the \textbf{-ve} in \emph{sīve}, \textquotedblleft{}or if,\textquotedblright{} and Marathi still carries it compounded inside \textbf{\hi{किंवा}} — \emph{kim} + \emph{vā}, \textquotedblleft{}what-or.\textquotedblright{} One old word, three descendants.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy yā dūdh?}
  \item the same pair with \emph{aur}, and hear the offer become a list
  \item which of the two you can also WRITE today — \textbf{\hi{या}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two joining words makes the listener choose? (\textbf{\hi{या}}.) Which Sanskrit particle is it? (\textbf{\hi{वा}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AF\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \hi{या}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lekin]{\hi{लेकिन} (\emph{lekin}) — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C68-lekin}



\begin{quote}
Two joining words are yours: \emph{aur} adds, \textbf{\hi{या}} offers. Both are agreeable. Neither can disagree with anything, and until one of them can, every sentence you build only ever confirms itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{लेकिन}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}} — \emph{lekin} — \textbf{but}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{है} \hi{लेकिन} \hi{दूध} \hi{नहीं} \hi{है}.} — \emph{chāy hai lekin dūdh nahīṁ hai.} — \textbf{There is tea but there is no milk.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}} takes the same slot as the other two and does the one thing they cannot: it lets the second half push back against the first. Notice that neither half changed — \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} is doing its own separate work inside the second clause, and \textbf{\hi{लेकिन}} only says how the two halves stand to each other.

Every letter in it is one you have: \textbf{\hi{ल}}, \textbf{\hi{े}}, \textbf{\hi{क}}, \textbf{\hi{ि}}, \textbf{\hi{न}}.

\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}} is Arabic — \textbf{\ar{لكن}} (\emph{lākin}) — and it walked into Hindi through Persian, in the same company as \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}}. Beside it Hindi keeps the inherited \textbf{\hi{पर}}, from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{परम्}}, \textquotedblleft{}beyond.\textquotedblright{} Two words for \emph{but}, one Persianate and one Sanskritic, is exactly what this language looks like: it almost never replaced a word, it collected a second one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy hai lekin dūdh nahīṁ hai}
  \item the three joiners in a row — \emph{aur}, \emph{yā}, \emph{lekin}
  \item the other Hindi word for \emph{but}, the inherited one — \emph{par}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joining word lets the second half disagree with the first? (\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}}.) Which language did Hindi take it from, and through which? (\textbf{Arabic, through Persian}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A5\%87\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A8}{Wiktionary: \hi{लेकिन}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… aur … · … yā … · … lekin …]{The same gap, three ways}

\label{lesson:HI-R68-three-joins}



\begin{quote}
Three words landed in this chapter and all three go in the same place. Name them in the order you met them, and say which one you cannot yet write.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāy aur dūdh}
  \item \emph{chāy yā dūdh?}
  \item \emph{chāy hai lekin dūdh nahīṁ hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one hands over both? (\emph{\textbf{aur}}.) Which makes you pick? (\textbf{\hi{या}}.) Which takes something back? (\textbf{\hi{लेकिन}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
